Particular
par-TIK-yoo-lur
a. (relating to a single person or thing, as distinguished from others; individual; specific)
Latin particula, a small part, diminutive of pars, a part. What is particular is, at root, a matter reduced to its individual pieces rather than considered as a whole.

Biblical Definition

Acts uses the word of Paul's own report to James and the elders at Jerusalem: called to account for a ministry many had heard rumors of, Paul does not summarize in general terms but declared particularly what things God had wrought among the Gentiles by his ministry — item by item, case by case, so that the elders could weigh the specific facts rather than the general reputation. Particularity here is a form of honesty; a man willing to be specific is a man willing to be checked.

Paul's other use of the word, to the Corinthians, applies the same precision to the body of Christ itself: Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular. The doctrine of the body only holds together because both halves are equally true — the church is one body, and every believer in it is a distinct, particular, individually named member of it, with a particular gift and a particular function that no other member can supply in his place. A theology of the church that only ever speaks generally, never particularly, has lost exactly the thing Paul insists on in the same breath he insists on the body's unity: the whole is real, and so, without contradiction, is every particular part of it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): relating to a single person or thing; individual; distinct from others; not general; specific.

expand to see more

PARTICULAR, a. Individual; distinct from others; noting a single thing or person, as opposed to general or universal.

MEMBER, n. A part of an animal body, as an arm, leg, or organ; figuratively, an individual of a body or society.

DECLARE, v.t. To make clear or manifest; to make known explicitly; to publish, or proclaim distinctly.

MINISTRY, n. The office, duties, or functions of a minister, particularly one appointed to teach and administer the gospel.

BODY, n. A collective mass; a number of individuals or particulars united or considered as one whole.

Key Scripture

Act 21:19 — "And when he had saluted them, he declared particularly what things God had wrought among the Gentiles by his ministry."

Act 21:20 — "And when they heard it, they glorified the Lord, and said unto him, Thou seest, brother, how many thousands of Jews there are which believe; and they are all zealous of the law:"

1Co 12:27 — "Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular."

1Co 12:12 — "For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ."

Modern Corruption

Particular is treated as the opposite of significant, the merely local detail set against the important general picture, when Acts uses it precisely to mean the kind of accountable specificity that lets a claim actually be tested.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; particular still names the individual instance rather than the general class. The principle worth recovering is Paul's own use of it before the Jerusalem elders: a man with nothing to hide is a man willing to be particular, to name the actual cases rather than rest on a general and unfalsifiable claim to have done a great work.

First Corinthians applies the same precision to church life, and refuses to let the doctrine of one body dissolve any believer's particular identity into an undifferentiated mass. Every member is named in particular, with a particular gift, in the very passage that most insists on the unity of the whole. A church that speaks only in generalities about the body of Christ, never in particulars about its actual members and their actual gifts, has not honored the doctrine Paul is teaching — it has quietly dropped half of it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kata heis hekastos (G1520/G1538), one by one, each severally; the phrase behind “in particular” in 1 Corinthians 12:27.

expand to see more

Greek kata heis (G2596/G1520) — according to one, one by one; the idiom behind “in particular” in 1 Corinthians 12:27.

Greek melos (G3196) — a member, a limb; the noun naming each particular part of the one body.

Greek kathexes (G2517) — in order, one after another; the manner Paul elsewhere reports things (Luke 1:3), close kin to the particularity of Acts 21:19.

Greek diegeomai (G1334) — to relate fully, to declare in detail; the sense behind “declared particularly.”

Greek ethnos (G1484) — a nation, a Gentile; the object of the particular things God had wrought through Paul's ministry.

Usage

"“he declared particularly what things God had wrought among the Gentiles” — Paul's accountable report at Jerusalem."

"“ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular” — the individual standing of every believer within the one body."

"“the body is one, and hath many members” — the unity that particularity never dissolves."
